doc.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025

title: Perry Robinson, avant garde and the start of Katrina
summary: White tells how Robinson told him there are no mistakes, leading to Vision Festival and Israel gigs, and his link between early New Orleans jazz and the avant garde.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Like Kidd Jordan down there, right?

Yes. And he kind of found that out near the end. But for most of my life I didn’t like it. People thought I couldn’t get into that and this, that and the other. But I met a clarinet player, Perry Robinson, who was from New York and he was an underground legend of the loft movement of the ‘60s and he played and recorded with a number of people in the avant garde vein. He was an older guy, and he came down to New Orleans to play. And, long story short, I sat in with him and he kept asking me to sit in. There were not a lot of people in the audience so I said what the heck. And I said, but man I’m really a traditional New Orleans player and I don't know anything about this stuff you’re doing. And he said that one thing that was also life changing – he said don’t worry about it, there are no mistakes in this music. And I was like huh? No mistakes? And that gave me the confidence to go on. And I started playing that, and I ended up playing a festival with him, the Vision Festival in New York, playing avant garde. I did it in Israel. I met an old legendary clarinet player there named Harold Rubin, and I also played with Perry in New York a few other times, and you know part of what I compose is in that vein. And you know I hear, strangely, a relationship between early New Orleans jazz and avant garde. And I like it. The reason I really could relate to it I think, I started listening to Albert Ayler you know, “Ghosts and Spirits” and all that. But I started playing with an African balafon player who had a band, and you know I had to learn how to play – improvise and play solos on one chord. You know? And over different kinds of rhythms. And that leaned toward avant garde. So at the same time I was, like thousands of other people, severely affected by hurricane Katrina. I lost my home, everything, it cost years of trying © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
